extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of philosophy of humor/film studies; philosophers interested in ethics and aesthetics of comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical analysis of why viewers laugh at ethically transgressive actions in films, focusing on the roles of incongruity, point of view, and partiality (with His Girl Friday as central case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity Thesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruity Thesis: the intentional content of S’s amusement is to be found in S’s believing or imagining that an incongruous state of affairs obtains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The basic idea: we live expecting patterns; we laugh when something doesn’t fit those patterns. Incongruity explains many features of humor (uniquely human, cross-cultural variability, catalyst of social change) but does not by itself tell which incongruities are amusing (some frighten or provoke curiosity). Examples: mistaken identity, riddles, meta-jokes. Criticisms and attempts to refine the notion of incongruity are noted (references to Hutcheson, Morreall, Scruton, Feinberg).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transgressive actions as a subclass of incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: One subset of incongruous events comprises transgressive events—events that appear to cross ethical boundaries (ostensibly wrong or bad)—and a great deal of successful humor concerns such transgressive actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: jokes whose punch lines involve strangling one's spouse; clown and Three Stooges physical abuse; films like Eating Raoul, Arsenic and Old Lace, Kind Hearts and Coronets, Monty Python scenes. The transgressiveness often contributes centrally to the humor rather than being incidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: humor about transgressions vs. transgressive jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between jokes that are about transgressive actions (laughing at wrongdoing) and jokes that are themselves transgressive (inviting laughter at tragic or taboo subjects without being about a wrongdoing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of the latter: 'One good thing about Alzheimer’s disease is that if you get it you can hide your own Easter eggs.' That joke is transgressive in inviting laughter at suffering rather than depicting a wrongdoing. This classification matters for explanation and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transgressiveness must often be preserved (not neutralized)
rubrics_metrics.description: For many examples of humor at wrongdoing, the very transgressiveness of the events involved is something we are laughing at; the wrong is not incidental but essential to the amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any satisfactory account must accommodate that a viewer who finds the film funny does not thereby think the wrongdoing is morally acceptable. Examples: Walter framing Bruce and kidnapping his mother in His Girl Friday—these wrongs are essential to their being funny; if the protagonist merely pleaded, the humor would be different or absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictionality/verity: neither necessary nor sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A wrongdoing’s being fictional is neither necessary nor sufficient for it to be humorous; sometimes verity (actual occurrence) strengthens amusement (e.g., hidden camera, realized practical jokes), while many fictional portrayals are equally or more amusing whether or not they are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hidden-camera comedy and Sacha Baron Cohen rely on verity; His Girl Friday likely unaffected by a title card claiming truth. But knowing a real crime occurred can make certain portrayals offensive rather than funny (e.g., real serial murder). The role of factuality depends on portrayal and point of view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view / portrayal requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Amusement depends centrally upon the point of view from which the transgressive action is presented; the point of view must lead to mirth rather than pity or anger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Components: (a) the portrayal must not neutralize the wrongness (the wrongness often contributes to incongruity); (b) the portrayal may or may not foreground fictionalness; (c) the specific framing/contextualization (what the spectator is shown and how) determines whether an incongruity yields amusement, fear, curiosity, or disgust. Thus identifying the relevant norms/expectations being violated is crucial (e.g., Walter pretending to mistake someone's identity is funny because he is intentionally acting for Hildy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Partiality in Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: A person’s being amused at something is significantly correlated with the person’s partiality toward or away from certain features of the humorous situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulation: amusement tends to correspond with being disposed toward the joker/performer and/or disposed against the butt of the joke, and magnitudes co-vary. The paper notes exceptions and does not overstate the principle; it holds generally rather than universally. Empirical and everyday observations support it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-grouping function of humor (laughter of inclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor often serves group-integration functions: laughing at outsiders reinforces in-group cohesion and partiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites sociological and psychological literature: laughter of inclusion, political cartoons and ridicule used to garner favor, and the role of amusement in consolidating group morale. Implication: humor can be instrumentally used to generate partiality and exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal influence: amusement affects partiality and vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: Being amused can make one more partial toward the source of amusement (or against the target), and existing partiality toward someone can increase one's mirth at jokes about others or at that person's transgressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and evidence: children mock others to gain popularity; experiments where faculty/students find pies thrown at their own out-group funnier; experimenter treated rudely vs politely—subjects who were treated rudely found the experimenter spilling hot tea funnier. Zillmann's summary: more intense negative disposition > greater mirth at disparagement; more intense positive disposition toward an agent > greater mirth when agent is butt/actor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partiality as explanatory mechanism in film (case: His Girl Friday)
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain films, the spectator’s partiality toward a perpetrator explains why we laugh with the perpetrator at his transgressions; the narrative actively develops and exploits this partiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In His Girl Friday, early teasing and private-show interactions incline viewers to side with Walter over Bruce; this allegiance suppresses affective acknowledgement of Walter’s wrongdoing, allowing the comedy to function. The film’s success depends on keeping spectator partiality toward Walter unshaken; if the viewer is put off by Walter, the comedic effect fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional (affective) vs cognitive awareness of wrongdoing
rubrics_metrics.description: Viewers may retain cognitive knowledge that wrongdoing occurred while lacking an affective acknowledgment (emotional awareness) of its wrongness, due to partiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues that the film 'hides' Walter’s transgressions in our partiality: we know he put Bruce in jail, and we know it's wrong, but we lack the affective disturbance (e.g., indignation) because amusement and allegiance 'play down' the wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different narrative roles for partiality (victim-oriented laughter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Partiality can also be toward victims (not perpetrators) in some comedies; the role of partiality in producing amusement varies by narrative and may not always explain laughter at victimization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chaplin, Buster Keaton, The Big Lebowski, The Jerk—these elicit sympathy for victims while still producing laughter. Partiality toward a victim may need to be overridden (e.g., belief in the character’s resiliency) or combined with other factors to allow laughter. The paper acknowledges this complexity and suggests more work is needed to specify conditions where partiality contributes differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a satisfactory account of humor at transgressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Any acceptable explanatory account must respect that (a) the transgressiveness often contributes centrally to the amusement, and (b) viewers do not thereby endorse the transgression morally; it must explain how amusement at transgressions is possible and not itself wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper focuses on the descriptive/explanatory question (what is going on when we find wrongdoings humorous) and leaves normative question (why is our doing so not itself wrong) for future work. It contrasts accounts like Freeland's (pleasure in spectacle) and Carroll's (pleasure as instrumentally tied to narrative disclosure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of incongruity: need to specify which incongruities produce amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all incongruities are amusing—some produce fear, curiosity, or disgust—so an account must specify which kinds of incongruity give rise to amusement rather than other responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes the unresolved task of making precise the notion of incongruity and the kinds that engender humor (references to Morreall, Feinberg, Scruton). Practical method: identify violated expectations/norms and how the portrayal frames them.
